questions.q: What architectural question does governance automation answer, building directly on Lesson 19's policy as code?
options: Where and when a policy-as-code check actually gets run, without a human remembering to run it
How to write a policy in Rego syntax for the first time
Whether encryption should be used at rest or in transit
How many roles an RBAC system should define
questions.explain: Lesson 19 covered writing policy as code; this lesson covers getting that code to actually execute against real resources on a trigger.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three places this lesson says automated governance checks get inserted?
options: A quarterly in-person committee vote
CI/CD pipeline checks
Scheduled compliance scans
Event-triggered checks
questions.explain: The three insertion points are CI/CD pipelines, scheduled scans, and event triggers — not a quarterly committee vote.

questions.q: What does a scheduled compliance scan catch that a CI/CD pipeline check would not?
options: Policy drift — a manual change made to an already-deployed resource, outside any pipeline
Syntax errors in the policy file itself
Network latency issues
Changes that are still in a pull request and haven't merged yet
questions.explain: A CI/CD check only fires on proposed changes going through the pipeline; a scheduled scan catches changes made directly to already-deployed resources.

questions.q: What is the difference between detection-only and automated remediation?
options: Detection-only reports a violation for a human to act on; automated remediation fixes the violation directly with no human in the loop
Detection-only is always more expensive to run than automated remediation
Automated remediation only works with CI/CD pipelines, never scheduled scans
There is no practical difference between the two
questions.explain: Detection surfaces the problem; remediation acts on it automatically — the lesson treats these as clearly distinct levels of automation.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say most real governance automation architectures start with detection-only rather than automated remediation?
options: An automated fix applied with no human review can cause its own outage if it's wrong, so remediation should be earned by a specific, proven-reliable check over time
Detection-only is required by law in every jurisdiction
Automated remediation is technically impossible to build
Detection-only requires no policy-as-code infrastructure at all
questions.explain: The lesson's explicit caution is that an unreviewed automated fix can itself cause an outage, so remediation is adopted gradually and deliberately, not by default.
